title: Ayesha Kapur Returns to Bollywood 17 Years After 'Black'
excerpt: The actor, who won a Filmfare Award at 11 for playing young Michelle in Sanjay Leela Bhansali's 'Black,' returns to the big screen in 'Om Ka Hari' — telling Hindustan Times the post-'Black' chatter once derailed her decision-making.
body:
• Ayesha Kapur, who won a Filmfare Award at 11 for playing young Michelle in Sanjay Leela Bhansali's "Black" (2005), has returned to Hindi cinema after a 17-year gap with the family drama "Om Ka Hari."
  • In an interview with Hindustan Times, she said the intense industry chatter after "Black" — with many people trying to "launch" her — affected her decision-making when she was too young to understand what that meant.
  • The long break now works in her favor, she says: audiences can see her as an adult actor rather than "that girl from Black." Her new role, an Indian girl from a small town and a middle-class family, is unlike anything she has played.
  • "Om Ka Hari," directed by Harish Vyas and co-starring Anshuman Jha, Raghubir Yadav and Soni Razdan, is currently running in theatres.

Ayesha Kapur is back on the big screen. Seventeen years after her last film appearance, the actor who played the young Michelle in Sanjay Leela Bhansali's Black has returned to Hindi cinema with Om Ka Hari, a family drama directed by Harish Vyas that is currently running in theatres. In a new interview with Hindustan Times, Kapur spoke candidly about the cost of early fame — and why walking away may have been the best decision of her career.

The child star who stepped away

Kapur was barely 10 when she won over audiences and critics as the young Michelle — the younger version of Rani Mukerji's character — in Black (2005), opposite Amitabh Bachchan. The performance earned her the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress at the 51st Filmfare Awards when she was 11. Four years later she appeared alongside Parzan Dastur in Sikandar (2009). Then she disappeared from films.

What followed was not a fall from grace but a deliberate withdrawal. A comeback vehicle once seemed close: she was attached to Shekhar Kapur's long-gestating Paani, opposite the late Sushant Singh Rajput, but the film never took off. In 2022 she announced a return with Hari Ka Om — the project that has now arrived in theatres as Om Ka Hari, after a shoot that began in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.

How the chatter shaped her choices

The most revealing part of the interview is Kapur's account of what the success of Black did to her as a child. "I have experienced people wanting to launch me. I also struggled with the concept. I was very young and didn't really know what that meant, and listening to people around me and the chatter affected my decision-making at the time," she said. "Now, I no longer let that affect me. I choose projects that I enjoy doing with people that I enjoy working with. That's just more my vibe."

"I choose projects that I enjoy doing with people that I enjoy working with. That's just more my vibe."

— Ayesha Kapur, actor

It is a frank description of a dynamic the industry rarely discusses: the machinery that forms around a child star, with adults making career decisions on behalf of someone too young to consent to them. Kapur's version of events is not bitter — she frames the hiatus as something that gave her room to grow up outside the glare.

Breaking the image of Michelle

That distance, she argues, is now an asset. "The break definitely allows people to see me as an adult in a film, separately from that girl from Black," she said. "Of course, people still remember that for some reason. It's still in people's hearts."

Om Ka Hari helps: her character is an Indian girl from a small town and a middle-class family, which Kapur describes as "very different from anything I have done before. I am excited to show a different side of me." The film co-stars Anshuman Jha, Raghubir Yadav, Soni Razdan and Manu Rishi Chaddha.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=b-bkoBrq9p8

Kapur prepared for the return methodically. Born in Düsseldorf, Germany, to Dilip Kapur — the founder of the leather-goods brand Hidesign — and raised in Auroville, Tamil Nadu, she studied at Columbia University in New York and worked for nearly six months on her Hindi diction with Kulvinder Bakshish, the language coach who trained Aamir Khan in Punjabi for Laal Singh Chaddha. Away from acting she built a separate career as an integrative nutrition health coach, and in March 2025 she married her longtime partner Adam Oberoi in Delhi.

What's next

Kapur is under no illusion that one film erases two decades of absence. "I just hope I get more chances to keep working, keep acting, and exploring," she said — a modest ambition that, after 17 years away, sounds like the point. If Om Ka Hari lands, the actor who was once frozen in the public memory as an 11-year-old prodigy gets to do something rarer than a comeback: start over as an adult.

Her story carries a particular resonance for the diaspora. Born in Germany, raised in Tamil Nadu, educated in New York and now working in Mumbai, Kapur's cross-continental life mirrors the back-and-forth many Indian families abroad live daily — and her account of childhood fame, adult interference and the choice to step back will be familiar to any parent who has watched a talented child navigate other people's ambitions.
